items.name: t-tests
items.about: Compares the averages of two groups, or two measurements from the same people, to see whether the gap is bigger than chance would produce.

items.name: ANOVA and mixed ANOVA
items.about: Compares averages across three or more groups. A mixed ANOVA also follows the same people across time or conditions.

items.name: Repeated-measures ANOVA
items.about: Compares the same people across several time points or conditions, so each person serves as their own comparison.

items.name: Chi-square tests
items.about: Tests whether counts in categories, such as yes and no by group, differ more than chance would predict.

items.name: Planned contrasts
items.about: Tests a specific comparison chosen before the data came in, such as one condition against the average of the others.

items.name: Effect sizes
items.about: Reports how large a difference or relationship is, not only whether it is statistically significant.

items.name: Crossover trial analysis
items.about: Analyzes a study in which each person gets every treatment in turn, accounting for order and for effects that carry over.

items.name: Linear regression
items.about: Estimates how a numeric outcome changes as one or more predictors change, holding the others constant.

items.name: Logistic regression
items.about: Models the odds of a yes-or-no outcome as predictors change.

items.name: Ordinal regression
items.about: Models an outcome with ordered categories, such as strongly disagree to strongly agree, without treating the steps as equal.

items.name: Negative-binomial regression
items.about: Models counts, such as the number of risky events, when the counts vary more than a simple count model allows.

items.name: Forward stepwise regression
items.about: Builds a model by adding predictors one at a time, keeping each only if it improves the fit.

items.name: Mixed-effects logistic regression
items.about: Models a yes-or-no outcome when the same people or groups contribute several observations.

items.name: Dominance and all-subsets analysis
items.about: Compares predictors by fitting every possible combination and measuring how much each one adds to explaining the outcome.

items.name: Multilevel (mixed-effects) models
items.about: Models data that come in clusters, such as repeated answers from one person or students in one class, using random effects.

items.name: Person-mean centering
items.about: Splits each person's score into their own average and their ups and downs around it, so within-person and between-person effects separate.

items.name: Lagged predictors and week effects
items.about: Uses an earlier time point to predict the next one, and adds a term for each week to absorb shifts shared by everyone.

items.name: Diary and experience-sampling analysis
items.about: Analyzes short surveys that people answer many times over days or weeks, to study how things change within a person.

items.name: Latent growth models
items.about: Models how scores change over time, with each person having their own starting level and rate of change.

items.name: Moderation and interactions
items.about: Tests whether the effect of one variable gets stronger or weaker depending on another.

items.name: Causal mediation (ACME)
items.about: Estimates how much of an effect passes through a middle step, called the average causal mediation effect.

items.name: Multilevel mediation
items.about: Tests a middle step when the data are clustered, separating effects within people from effects between people.

items.name: Mediated moderation
items.about: Tests whether a middle step explains why an effect is stronger for some people than for others.

items.name: Subgroup analysis
items.about: Compares an outcome, or a relationship, across groups of people to see whether it holds in each one.

items.name: Randomized experiments
items.about: Assigns people to conditions by chance, so differences in outcomes can be traced to the condition.

items.name: Propensity-score matching
items.about: Pairs treated and untreated people who look alike on recorded traits, so they can be compared more fairly when assignment was not random.

items.name: Difference-in-differences
items.about: Compares the before-and-after change in a treated group with the change in a comparison group.
items.mine: I have used it in the structure of randomized before-and-after studies, not on observational data.

items.name: Regression discontinuity
items.about: Compares people just above and just below a cutoff to estimate the effect of being past it.
items.mine: I used it on CSUN student records at the 15-unit load cutoff, then followed it with propensity-score matching.

items.name: Instrumental variables
items.about: Uses a factor that moves the treatment but affects the outcome only through it, to estimate a causal effect when assignment was not random.
items.mine: I learned it in graduate coursework.

items.name: Exploratory factor analysis
items.about: Looks for how many underlying ideas a set of questions captures, and lets the data suggest the groupings.

items.name: Confirmatory factor analysis
items.about: Tests whether a set of questions groups into the underlying ideas a theory predicts, and how well that structure fits.

items.name: Reliability and validity testing
items.about: Checks whether a measure gives consistent results and whether it captures what it claims to capture.

items.name: Structural equation and path models
items.about: Tests a whole network of relationships among measured and unmeasured variables at once, and checks how well it fits.

items.name: Multi-group models
items.about: Tests whether a measurement or path model works the same way across groups.

items.name: Latent profile analysis
items.about: Finds hidden subgroups of people who share a pattern across several measures.

items.name: Power and sensitivity analysis
items.about: Estimates how many people a study needs to detect an effect of a given size, or which effect sizes a finished study could detect.

items.name: Specification-curve analysis
items.about: Runs every reasonable version of an analysis and shows how the result changes across them.

items.name: Bonferroni and Tukey corrections
items.about: Adjust significance tests when many comparisons are made, so false positives stay under control.

items.name: Variance inflation checks
items.about: Check whether predictors overlap so much that a regression's estimates become unstable.

items.name: Intent-to-treat analysis
items.about: Analyzes people in the group they were assigned to, even if they did not follow it, which keeps random assignment intact.

items.name: Blind outcome rating
items.about: Has judges score work without knowing which condition produced it.

items.name: Bayes factors
items.about: Express how strongly the data favor one hypothesis over another, including evidence for no effect.

items.name: Bayesian t-tests
items.about: Compare two group averages with a Bayes factor, which can show support for no difference.

items.name: Dictionary-based text analysis (LIWC)
items.about: Counts words from fixed lists, such as emotion or social words, to measure what a piece of writing is about.

items.name: Text-similarity metrics
items.about: Score how alike two texts are, for example by shared words (Jaccard, Sørensen-Dice) or word-count vectors (cosine).

items.name: TF-IDF and bag of words
items.about: Turn text into word counts. TF-IDF gives more weight to words that set one document apart from the others.

items.name: Topic models and embeddings
items.about: Find themes across many documents, or turn meaning into numbers so similar texts sit close together.

items.name: Classification trees
items.about: Predict a category by splitting cases through a series of yes-or-no questions about their features.

items.name: Support vector machines
items.about: Predict a category by finding the boundary that best separates the groups of cases.

items.name: Nearest neighbors
items.about: Predict a case's category from the categories of the most similar cases.

items.name: Naive Bayes
items.about: Predict a category by combining the odds from each feature, assuming the features act independently.

items.name: Cross-validation
items.about: Test a model on data it was not trained on, by repeatedly holding out part of the data.

items.name: ROC curves and confusion matrices
items.about: Show how often a classifier is right and in what ways it is wrong, across different cutoffs.

items.name: Pooled raw-data analysis
items.about: Combines the raw data from several studies into one model, rather than averaging published results.

items.name: Data harmonization
items.about: Matches measures, codes, and formats across studies so the data can be combined.

items.name: Geospatial mapping
items.about: Maps data tied to places to see how outcomes vary by location.

items.name: Cost-benefit analysis
items.about: Compares what a program costs with the value of what it produces.
